description: Mathematics Year 6 width tiers lookup — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor. Generated from ACARA elaborations and width_generation_prompt v1.0.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term. For concept/understanding standards: the minimum number of phenomena or contexts that satisfies the command term. For modelling/capability standards: the narrowest task context that genuinely meets the descriptor. Must certify the descriptor is 'met' — not merely familiar territory.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended. Grounded in the main elaboration cases. Reflects what a well-taught Year 6 class that has engaged seriously with the descriptor would have done. Does not require every elaboration to be covered.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, cultural contexts, or application domains — not harder versions of the same context. Each item is a discrete enrichment direction. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: Verbatim ACARA elaborations reproduced as source data for traceability. Elaborations are examples of how the descriptor might be addressed — they are source data, not a checklist.

AC9M6N01.minimum_width: Recognise integers in at least two real-world contexts (e.g. temperature, finance); locate positive and negative integers on a number line; identify coordinate positions in two quadrants of the Cartesian plane.
AC9M6N01.typical_width: Recognise integers across a range of everyday contexts including temperature, altitude, profit/loss, and timeline positions; locate and order integers on a number line; represent integer coordinates in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane; connect positive/negative direction to coordinate sign.
wider: Investigate integers in scientific contexts including planetary temperatures, sea-level measurements, and electrical charge
Apply integer coordinate reasoning to map-reading, orienteering, or game-board contexts using all four quadrants
Explore historical development of negative numbers — when were they formally accepted and why were they controversial?
elaborations: extending the number line in the negative direction to locate and represent integers, recognising the difference in location between negative and positive integers
using integers to represent quantities in financial contexts, including the concept of profit and loss for a planned event
using horizontal and vertical number lines to represent and find solutions to everyday problems involving locating and ordering integers around zero
recognising that the sign (positive or negative) indicates a direction in relation to zero
representing the temperatures of the different planets in the solar system, using a diagram of a thermometer that models a vertical number line

AC9M6N02.minimum_width: Identify whether a number is prime or composite using factor analysis; express a composite number as a product of prime factors using a factor tree; identify the first 12 square numbers.
AC9M6N02.typical_width: Identify prime and composite numbers to 100 including using the Sieve of Eratosthenes; express composite numbers as products of prime factors; identify square numbers and their square roots to 144; use prime factorisation to simplify calculations such as finding common factors.
wider: Investigate patterns in the distribution of primes using the Sieve of Eratosthenes — twin primes, gaps between primes, the thinning of prime density
Explore the connection between prime factorisation and simplifying fractions, finding HCF and LCM
Investigate square number patterns including the consecutive odd number sum pattern (1=1², 1+3=2², 1+3+5=3²...) and triangular numbers as a comparison
elaborations: using the definition of a prime number to explain why one is not a prime number
testing numbers by using division to distinguish between prime and composite numbers, recording the results on a number chart to identify any patterns
representing composite numbers as a product of their factors, including prime factors when necessary and using this form to simplify calculations
identifying and describing the product of a number with itself as square
using spreadsheets to list all the numbers that have up to 3 factors, recognise any emerging patterns

AC9M6N03.minimum_width: Find equivalent fractions for halves, thirds and quarters; find a common denominator for two fractions with different denominators; order at least five common fractions on a number line with justification.
AC9M6N03.typical_width: Generate equivalent fractions; find lowest common denominators for pairs of common fractions; order a set of fractions including halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths on the same number line; justify ordering using equivalence reasoning; apply benchmark fractions for estimation.
wider: Extend ordering to include mixed numerals and improper fractions on the same number line
Investigate the density property of fractions — between any two fractions, can you always find another? Demonstrate and explain.
Connect fraction ordering to decimal equivalents — plot fractions and their decimal forms on the same number line and discuss the relationship
elaborations: applying factors and multiples to fraction denominators, such as halves with quarters, eighths and twelfths, and thirds with sixths, ninths and twelfths
representing fractions on the same number line, paying attention to relative position, and using this to explain relationships between denominators
explaining equivalence and order between fractions using number lines, drawings and models
comparing and ordering fractions by placing cards on a string line across the room and referring to benchmark fractions to justify their position

AC9M6N04.minimum_width: Add and subtract pairs of decimal numbers with up to two decimal places using written algorithm with correct alignment; use rounding to check reasonableness.
AC9M6N04.typical_width: Add and subtract decimals with up to three decimal places using written algorithms, mental strategies (partitioning, compensation), and digital tools; select strategies based on calculation complexity; apply estimation and rounding to check reasonableness; work with measurement and financial contexts.
wider: Apply decimal addition and subtraction to linear measurement contexts including comparing records and targets expressed as decimals
Investigate multi-step decimal problems in financial or data contexts where totals must be calculated and checked
Explore when mental strategies are more efficient than written algorithms for decimal calculations and articulate the conditions
elaborations: applying estimation strategies to addition and subtraction of decimals to at least thousandths before calculating
applying whole-number strategies including basic facts, place value, partitioning and inverse relationships
working additively with linear measurements expressed as decimals up to 2 and 3 decimal places
deciding to use a calculator as a calculation strategy for solving additive problems involving decimals that vary in their number of decimal places

AC9M6N05.minimum_width: Add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator; handle mixed numeral addition and subtraction including cases requiring regrouping.
AC9M6N05.typical_width: Add and subtract fractions with unrelated denominators using lowest common denominators; add and subtract mixed numerals including cases requiring regrouping; apply to realistic problem contexts including measurement, cooking, and sharing; represent using number line or diagram.
wider: Solve multi-step problems requiring both addition and subtraction of fractions in a single problem chain
Investigate and compare strategies for adding mixed numerals (add parts separately vs convert to improper fractions first) and identify when each is more efficient
Apply fraction addition and subtraction to data and statistics contexts — e.g. combining fractional parts of a whole from a survey
elaborations: representing addition and subtraction of fractions using number lines and diagrams with understanding of equivalent fractions
determining the lowest common denominator using understanding of prime and composite numbers
calculating the addition or subtraction of fractions in realistic problem contexts
understanding the processes for adding and subtracting fractions with related denominators in preparation for calculating with unrelated denominators

AC9M6N06.minimum_width: Multiply and divide decimal numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 using place value reasoning; explain the effect in terms of digit place value shifts.
AC9M6N06.typical_width: Multiply and divide decimals by multiples of powers of 10 (e.g. 20, 300, 5000) using a two-step decomposition; apply to metric unit conversion; use estimation to check reasonableness; connect to multiplication facts combined with place value.
wider: Apply multiplying and dividing by powers of 10 to metric conversion chains (mm → cm → m → km) and explain the conversion factor at each step
Investigate the effect of multiplying a decimal by 0.1, 0.01 — connect to division by powers of 10
Apply powers-of-10 decimal operations to scientific notation and measurement contexts at an introductory level
elaborations: applying place value knowledge including that the value of the digit is 10 times smaller each time a place is moved to the right
applying and explaining estimation strategies in multiplicative situations involving a decimal multiplied by a two- or three-digit number
explaining the effect of multiplying or dividing a decimal by 10, 100, 1000 in terms of place value — not the decimal point shifting

AC9M6N07.minimum_width: Find a unit fraction of a whole number quantity; find a common percentage (10%, 25%, 50%) of a quantity; calculate a simple percentage discount and find the discounted price.
AC9M6N07.typical_width: Find any familiar fraction of a quantity; find common percentages (5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 33⅓%, 50%, 75%) of quantities using efficient mental strategies; calculate percentage discounts including composite discounts; apply to financial contexts including GST and sales prices.
wider: Investigate building any percentage from 10% and 1% components — develop a mental strategy that generalises to any percentage
Explore percentage calculations in financial contexts including GST, layby, savings, and comparing sale prices across different discount structures
Investigate reverse percentage problems — if 75% of a quantity is 60, what is the whole? — and develop reasoning strategies
elaborations: explaining how 1/3 of a quantity can be achieved by dividing by 3, and how 1/3 can be used to find other fractions of the same quantity
investigating percentage discounts of 15%, 30% and 45% using their decimal representations
linking percentages to their decimal equivalent of tenths and hundredths and using these to determine percentage discounts
explaining the equivalence between percentages and fractions including 33⅓% and 1/3
representing a situation with a mathematical expression involving finding a familiar fraction, decimal or percentage of a quantity

AC9M6N08.minimum_width: Round fractions and decimals to convenient values to estimate sums, differences, or percentages; use estimation to check whether a calculated answer is plausible.
AC9M6N08.typical_width: Apply multiple estimation strategies to problems involving rational numbers and percentages: rounding, benchmark fractions, 10%-building for percentages, front-end estimation; select the strategy best suited to the context; apply to financial contexts including budget estimates and price comparisons.
wider: Compare front-end, rounding, and benchmark strategies on the same set of problems — evaluate which produces closer estimates for different problem types
Investigate real financial contexts where estimation is the primary decision tool (shopping budgets, event planning) and discuss required precision
Explore how professionals use approximation — journalist rounding, builder quoting, scientist reporting — and discuss appropriate precision in each
elaborations: using familiar fractions, decimals and percentages to approximate calculations
recognising and using the most efficient strategies for solving problems, such as recognising that 48% is approximately 50% to make an estimate
using benchmark percentages to estimate the percentage of a quantity
using estimates of percentages to check the reasonableness of solutions
estimating the percentage of a shape that has been shaded
using estimation to check the reasonableness of calculations involving rational numbers and percentages in financial contexts

AC9M6N09.minimum_width: Formulate and solve a practical problem involving rational numbers or percentages; identify the operation(s) needed; interpret the result in context.
AC9M6N09.typical_width: Use the full modelling cycle (formulate → calculate → interpret → communicate → justify) for problems involving rational numbers and percentages; choose between mental, written, and digital strategies; interpret results with appropriate precision; communicate solutions as complete contextual responses.
wider: Apply mathematical modelling to multi-step financial planning tasks — budgeting, comparing options, calculating value for money
Investigate and communicate modelling solutions to an audience (partner, class) and respond to questions about strategy choices
Explore problems where the mathematical answer needs contextual interpretation — e.g. rounding up for packaging, rounding down for remaining budget
elaborations: modelling situations that represent mathematical problems involving natural numbers, integers, fractions, decimals and percentages
using mathematical modelling to solve practical problems including problems involving money and percentage discounts
interpreting and communicating solutions in terms of the situation, including justifying the reasonableness of conclusions

AC9M6A01.minimum_width: Identify the rule for a number pattern involving rational numbers and extend it; connect a visually growing pattern to a number sequence and predict future terms.
AC9M6A01.typical_width: Identify and describe rules for additive and multiplicative patterns involving decimals and fractions; connect visual growing patterns to the number rules generating them; represent patterns in tables of values and number sequences; use rules to predict non-adjacent terms.
wider: Use spreadsheets to generate and investigate long sequences and identify emerging patterns not visible in the first few terms
Investigate patterns from calculator experiments — division sequences (1÷9, 2÷9...), multiplication patterns — and describe the mathematical structure
Explore patterns from real-world contexts (compound growth, tiling, paper folding) and describe the rules generating them
elaborations: investigating patterns such as the number of tiles in a geometric pattern, or the number of dots or other shapes in successive repeats of a strip or border pattern
using a calculator or spreadsheet to experiment with number patterns from multiplying or dividing
creating extended number sequences representing additive patterns using decimals
investigating the number of regions created by successive folds of a sheet of paper
creating a pattern sequence with materials, writing the associated number sequence and describing the rule

AC9M6A02.minimum_width: Evaluate numerical expressions involving brackets and mixed operations; find unknown values in equations with brackets using inverse operations.
AC9M6A02.typical_width: Apply order-of-operations conventions including brackets to evaluate complex expressions; find unknowns in numerical equations with brackets using inverse operations and number properties (distributive, associative, commutative); verify solutions by substitution.
wider: Apply the distributive property as a mental calculation strategy — e.g. 6 × 99 = 6 × (100 − 1) — and investigate other applications
Investigate equations where the unknown appears in different structural positions and develop strategies for each
Explore how order-of-operations conventions function in calculator and spreadsheet contexts — when do they produce unexpected results?
elaborations: using brackets and order of operations to write number sentences and appreciating the need for agreed rules
constructing equivalent number sentences involving brackets and combinations of the 4 operations
finding pairs of unknown values in numerical equations that make the equation hold true
applying knowledge of inverse operations and number properties to create equivalent number sentences

AC9M6A03.minimum_width: Write an algorithm (as steps or flowchart) that uses a rule to generate a number sequence; trace through the algorithm to verify it produces the correct output; identify a pattern in the generated set.
AC9M6A03.typical_width: Create algorithms with decision branches to generate number sets using arithmetic rules, divisibility conditions, or combined criteria; test algorithms using digital tools; identify and explain patterns that emerge from the algorithm's rules; represent algorithms in written and flowchart form.
wider: Design algorithms to generate sequences with interesting mathematical properties (Fibonacci-like, prime-filter) and investigate the patterns
Investigate the Collatz conjecture algorithmically — test many starting values using a spreadsheet and describe observed patterns
Explore how algorithms with the same output can be structured differently — compare alternative algorithms for the same sequence
elaborations: using an algorithm to create extended number sequences involving rational numbers, using a rule and digital tools, explaining emerging patterns
designing an algorithm to model operations, using input and output concepts, describing and explaining relationships and patterns
designing an algorithm or simple program to generate a sequence based on user input and a chosen operation, discussing patterns

AC9M6M01.minimum_width: Convert between adjacent metric units for length (km/m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g), and capacity (L/mL) by multiplying or dividing by the appropriate power of 10; express two-unit measurements as decimals in the larger unit.
AC9M6M01.typical_width: Convert between adjacent and non-adjacent metric units across length, mass and capacity; select between decimal and two-unit representations based on context; connect metric conversion to place value and the prefix system; apply to measurement problem solving.
wider: Investigate the SI metric prefix system beyond kilo and milli — mega, giga, micro, nano — and connect to digital technology and scientific contexts
Apply metric conversion chains to unit analysis problems: how many millilitres in a kilolitre? Connect to powers-of-10 reasoning
Investigate historical contexts where unit system inconsistency caused errors — NASA Mars Climate Orbiter — and discuss the importance of unit consistency
elaborations: recognising the significance of the prefixes in units of measurement
identifying and using correct operations when converting between units
recognising the equivalence of measurements, such as 1.25 metres is the same as 125 centimetres

AC9M6M02.minimum_width: Establish the area formula for a rectangle using array reasoning; apply the formula to find the area of rectangles with whole number dimensions; state the result in square units.
AC9M6M02.typical_width: Establish and apply the area formula to rectangles with decimal dimensions; solve practical problems including finding area, finding a missing dimension given area, and decomposing compound shapes into rectangles; connect area to perimeter distinctions.
wider: Investigate the relationship between area and perimeter — rectangles with the same area can have different perimeters, and vice versa; explore systematically
Apply area reasoning to tiling and flooring problems with unit conversion (cm to m²)
Investigate First Nations Australian use of spatial reasoning and area in design, weaving, and land management — connect geometric principles to these contexts
elaborations: using one centimetre grid paper to construct rectangles, recording dimensions and areas in a table
using the relationship between square units and the array structure to derive a formula for area of a rectangle
solving problems involving comparison of lengths and areas using appropriate units
investigating the connection between perimeters of different rectangles with the same area

AC9M6M03.minimum_width: Read departure and arrival times from a timetable; calculate journey duration including cases crossing a time boundary; plan a simple two-leg itinerary.
AC9M6M03.typical_width: Extract information from timetables in 12- and 24-hour format; calculate durations using multiple strategies; plan multi-leg itineraries accounting for connection times and constraints; identify feasibility of planned schedules.
wider: Plan a real or simulated excursion itinerary with multiple activities, constraints, and buffer times — present as a formatted schedule
Investigate time zone calculations — connecting international travel times to time zone differences
Explore how timetable design choices affect usability and what conventions make public transport timetables readable
elaborations: planning a trip involving one or more modes of public transport
developing a timetable of daily activities for a planned event such as a sports carnival
investigating different ways duration is represented in timetables

AC9M6M04.minimum_width: Identify angles on a straight line (sum 180°), angles at a point (sum 360°), and vertically opposite angles (equal); find unknown angles using each relationship individually.
AC9M6M04.typical_width: Apply all three angle relationships to find unknown angles in diagrams; combine relationships for multi-step problems; communicate reasoning naming the property used at each step; verify by checking consistency of all angles in the diagram.
wider: Investigate where angle relationships appear in geometric figures — parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals — and explain the connections
Identify angle relationships in First Nations Australian art, Islamic geometric patterns, or architectural designs and describe them using geometric vocabulary
Explore how angle relationships are used in navigation — compass bearings, directional instructions
elaborations: using protractors or dynamic geometry software to measure and generalise about angles formed when lines are crossed
demonstrating the meaning of language associated with angle properties including complementary, supplementary, vertically opposite
using the properties of supplementary and complementary angles to represent spatial situations with number sentences and solving for unknown angles

AC9M6SP01.minimum_width: Identify the cross-sectional shape of common 3D objects; identify objects with constant parallel cross-sections (prisms) and explain what makes them prisms; classify a set of objects as prisms or non-prisms.
AC9M6SP01.typical_width: Identify and compare parallel cross-sections of a range of 3D objects; define and apply the constant cross-section criterion for right prisms; classify objects including cylinders and non-standard prisms; connect cross-section understanding to everyday structural and manufactured objects.
wider: Investigate the connection between constant cross-sections and volume — why does area × length work for prisms?
Explore cross-sections in real-world contexts: architecture, medical imaging (CT/MRI), engineering design
Investigate oblique prisms and whether they qualify under the constant cross-section definition
elaborations: using cross-sections of 3D objects to identify prisms and distinguish them from other objects
comparing parallel cross-sections of objects including rectangular prisms, triangular prisms, and cylinders
recognising that right prisms have the same cross-section along their length
identifying prism structures in everyday objects and architecture
connecting cross-sections to the faces and nets of prisms
investigating how changing the cross-section shape produces a different prism

AC9M6SP02.minimum_width: Plot points with integer coordinates in all four quadrants; read coordinates in all four quadrants; describe which coordinate changes when a point moves horizontally or vertically.
AC9M6SP02.typical_width: Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants including on axes; predict new coordinates after described movements; describe coordinate changes for movements that cross axes; connect coordinate change to integer addition.
wider: Investigate reflections across the axes — identify the sign pattern for coordinate changes and generalise
Apply four-quadrant coordinates to map or game-board contexts with a real reference point
Explore systematic translations of shapes — if all vertices move by the same amount, describe the resulting coordinate changes
elaborations: locating and plotting points with integer coordinates in all four quadrants
describing the movement required to move from one point to another in the Cartesian plane
identifying how the coordinates change when a point is moved to a new location
recognising that coordinates can be negative when a point is located to the left of or below the origin
connecting coordinate movement to integer addition and subtraction
using the Cartesian plane to represent and solve problems involving movement and position

AC9M6SP03.minimum_width: Apply two transformations in sequence to a shape and describe the combined effect; identify whether a regular polygon tessellates using the interior angle criterion; create a simple tessellation using one shape and one transformation.
AC9M6SP03.typical_width: Apply and describe combinations of translations, reflections, and rotations; identify the transformation rules generating given tessellations; create tessellations with combinations of transformations; use dynamic software to create and modify geometric patterns.
wider: Investigate and create patterns from First Nations Australian art or Islamic geometric traditions, identifying the transformation rules and explaining their mathematical structure
Create modified tessellations in the style of Escher by distorting a tessellating shape while preserving transformation properties
Investigate semi-regular tessellations combining two or more regular polygons and describe the transformation rules
elaborations: using combinations of transformations to create tessellations using digital tools
identifying which combinations of regular polygons can be used to tile a plane
describing and identifying the transformations used to create a tessellation
creating geometric patterns using combinations of transformations
connecting tessellations to cultural patterns and designs including First Nations Australian art

AC9M6ST01.minimum_width: Classify a variable by type (ordinal, nominal, discrete, continuous); select an appropriate display; calculate mode and range for a dataset; make two comparative statements between two datasets.
AC9M6ST01.typical_width: Classify variables across all four types; select and justify display types; calculate and interpret mode, range, and shape for multiple datasets; construct comparative displays; make specific comparative statements relating statistical features to context.
wider: Investigate comparative data from media sources (sports, health, surveys) and evaluate the claims made from distributions
Explore what median and mean could add to comparisons that mode and range miss — introduce informally through investigation
Compare distributions from First Nations Australian community data contexts, discussing what fair and respectful statistical comparison looks like
elaborations: using comparative displays such as side-by-side column graphs, dot plots and two-way tables to compare distributions
comparing distributions for the same variable across different groups
describing distributions in terms of mode, range and shape and using these to make comparisons
using digital tools to create comparative displays for ordinal, nominal, discrete and continuous data

AC9M6ST02.minimum_width: Identify a statistical claim in a media example; locate the data, representation, and conclusion; identify at least one potential problem with the method or representation.
AC9M6ST02.typical_width: Evaluate statistical arguments in traditional and digital media; identify issues with data collection (sample size, bias, question design) and representation (truncated axes, misleading scales, inappropriate display types); assess whether conclusions are supported by the evidence.
wider: Investigate published examples of misleading graphs and explain each technique's effect on how the data is perceived
Evaluate statistical arguments from public health, environmental, or social contexts — discuss what makes a statistical argument credible
Design both a misleading and a fair representation of the same dataset — compare and explain the choices made in each
elaborations: identifying statistical arguments presented in media including newspapers, magazines and digital sources
discussing and critiquing the methods used to collect and represent data in media
evaluating whether conclusions drawn from data are justified by the evidence
identifying potential sources of bias in data collection and representation

AC9M6ST03.minimum_width: Pose a statistical question; collect relevant data using a simple method; produce an appropriate display; state two findings that address the investigation question in context.
AC9M6ST03.typical_width: Use the full statistical investigation cycle: pose and refine question, design data collection, collect data systematically, analyse using mode/range/shape, interpret in context, communicate findings; acknowledge investigation limitations.
wider: Conduct investigations using secondary data sources including government or community datasets; compare primary and secondary data collection
Refine the investigation based on initial findings — pose and pursue a follow-up question
Communicate findings to a real or simulated audience and respond to questions about methods, limitations, and conclusions
elaborations: posing questions of interest about the class and wider community
deciding what data to collect and how to record it
representing data in a variety of ways and using digital tools to display, analyse and interpret data
refining the investigation question based on what the data reveals
communicating findings in a variety of ways including oral, written and digital reports
comparing results with initial expectations and considering what further investigation is needed

AC9M6P01.minimum_width: Place events on a 0–1 probability scale; express probability values as fractions, decimals and percentages; assign estimated probabilities to events in a given context with justification.
AC9M6P01.typical_width: Use the 0–1 (or 0–100%) scale to represent and compare probabilities; convert between fraction, decimal and percentage probability representations; assign estimated probabilities to events across a range of contexts; verify that complementary probabilities sum to 1.
wider: Investigate sports and weather forecasting contexts that use probability — what does '70% chance of rain' mean on the 0–1 scale?
Explore First Nations Australian games of chance and investigate the probability structures within them
Compare probability estimation in contexts where theoretical probability is known (dice, cards) vs unknown (weather, sport) and discuss what each requires
elaborations: identifying the chance of events occurring in familiar contexts and representing these chances on a scale from 0 to 1
discussing the relationship between the probability scale from 0 to 1 and percentages
assigning probabilities to events using fractions, decimals and percentages
using estimation to assign probabilities to events in everyday contexts
recognising that the probability of an event and its complement sum to 1
connecting probability language (impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain) to numerical values on the scale

AC9M6P02.minimum_width: Conduct a chance experiment and calculate experimental probability; compare to theoretical probability; describe how results change with more trials.
AC9M6P02.typical_width: Conduct repeated experiments; compare experimental probabilities at different trial counts (10, 50, 100+); identify the convergence trend; use digital simulation tools to run large numbers of trials; compare experimental frequency to expected frequency and discuss variation.
wider: Graph cumulative experimental probability against number of trials and describe the convergence pattern
Investigate the Gambler's Fallacy — explain why past results do not affect independent future events
Explore Monte Carlo simulation at an accessible level — using random trials to estimate a mathematical quantity (e.g. approximating π)
elaborations: conducting repeated chance experiments and recording results
using digital tools to simulate chance experiments with increasing numbers of trials
comparing the results of simulations with expected results
discussing the effect on variation of increasing the number of trials
